analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the 2001 and 2003 Bush tax cuts and repeals the estate tax permanently.
analysis.headline: The bill to make the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and repeal the estate tax got no cosponsors and never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would remove the expiration dates built into the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts, making the reduced income tax rates, lower taxes on dividends and capital gains, and other cuts permanent. It would also permanently repeal the federal estate tax for large inheritances and permanently raise the income threshold for the alternative minimum tax. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Households in the top income brackets gain the most, since the highest-rate tax cuts and the elimination of taxes on dividends, capital gains, and very large estates flow disproportionately to wealthy families and heirs. Middle-income households would also keep lower rates, but their share of the benefit is far smaller.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the 2010 expiration date on the 2001 tax act's rate cuts, child credit, marriage penalty relief, and other provisions, making them permanent [S2][S3].
Makes permanent the reduced tax rates on capital gains and dividends from the 2003 act, which go mostly to high-income investors [S2][S3].
Permanently repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, so very large inheritances pass untaxed [S2][S3].

Gradually raises the alternative minimum tax exemption through 2021 and lets most nonrefundable credits offset the AMT, protecting middle- and upper-middle-income families from a parallel tax system [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue falls substantially, and either deficits rise or other programs are cut eventually. Since the largest cuts go to high earners and large estates, the lost revenue is heavily concentrated in what those households would otherwise have paid.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no provision to replace the lost revenue, so it would substantially increase federal deficits and the national debt [S3].
By making the 2001 and 2003 rate cuts permanent, it locks in a tax structure whose largest dollar benefits accrue to the highest-income households [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Middle-income households would see modest tax savings and some protection from the AMT, but the bill's dominant effect is to permanently extend the largest cuts to top earners and to eliminate the estate tax entirely, with no offsetting revenue. On balance, it directs far more benefit to concentrated wealth than to typical working families.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 112th Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Pence introduced the bill on February 14, 2011 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on February 14, 2011 [S5].
No further action was taken; no hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo continued; no tax law changed, so taxpayers and the Treasury were no worse off because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died in committee.

for.name: Rep. Mike Pence
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought permanent extension of the 2001/2003 tax cuts and estate tax repeal.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican House member introduced the bill with no cosponsors listed, and it received no recorded action or votes.

industries.note: Would receive permanent rate cuts and full estate tax repeal, the largest shares of the bill's tax reductions.
